ledger.contains: Wayback Machine copy (15 July 2015) of the CBI Unit website page 'Grenada Real Estate': the real-estate option requires 'a minimum investment of USD 350,000' in designated real estate (already recorded as a term) and a list of five government-approved projects with contact details (The Levera Project, Mariposa, Mount Cinnamon Resort and Beach Club, The Point at Petite Calivigny, The Sanctuary at Fiji Beach); no count is printed, so nothing more to record. Note: the existing term t-d11adc5896 attributed to this source (government fee US$50,000 etc.) quotes the separate Fees page archived on 29 June 2015, which is not part of this stored file. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

One-page IMA Grenada 'The CEO's Desk: Processing Report' (2024): text on faster processing (two-track system separating backlog from new applications); a chart of 80 applications processed by processing time (1 to 6 months); a bar chart of applications processed in the first quarter of 2021-2024 (102, 120, 307, 388) with growth rates; annual applications processed 2021-2023 (430, 493, 1,581; already recorded). All numbers extracted except the printed growth rates (18%, 156%, 26%, 'over 300%', 223%), which are comparisons derived from the counts and are not recorded. The period covered by the 80-application chart is not stated (recorded as 2023-2024, basis unspecified). Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

IMF Country Report No. 25/39 (February 2025): 2024 Article IV consultation for Grenada, 97 pages. Programme content: Table 1 memo lines CBI inflows and government CBI revenue (percent of GDP) 2019-2029 (also repeated in Table 2); Table 3a (EC$m) and Table 3b (percent of GDP) lines 'Citizenship by Investment Program' (non-tax revenue), 'Bondholder CBI-related payments' and memo 'Government CBI revenue' 2019-2029; text: CBI revenue 10½% of GDP in 2023 (already recorded; repeated in the Executive Director's statement, PDF p. 95), Box 1 programme description (NTF US$235,000; real estate US$270,000 with five-year holding and US$50,000 government contribution, now recorded as terms; Russia/Belarus ban, regional MoA of March 2024 and IMA rebranding already recorded as events) and a scenario assumption (inflows 50% above/below baseline, an assumption, not recorded); policy advice to move all CBI revenue into the NTF; footnotes on bondholders' share of the previous year's CBI revenue, contingency fund transfers and escrow accumulation. All table lines now recorded for every year (two new indicators proposed for the bondholder payments). Not recorded because they are not CBI-only: capital account inflows of 9.5% (2023) and 15% (2024) of GDP 'largely due to the NTF component of CBI', government deposits of 22-23% of GDP, the 2024-25 external accounts text table. Box 1 charts (PDF p. 16) have no printed values. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

IMF first ECF review for Grenada (Dec 2014). Annex II on the new CBI programme: visa-free access table (event exists), fee schedule as of August 2014 (NTF and private-investment rows already recorded; the two 'tranche' rows added as terms), the rule that all budget fees are saved (25-100% of public-sector inflows; added as event), the NTF's monthly EC$2 million transfer for arrears (added as event), and a staff estimate that budget receipts could be 0.2-0.6% of GDP a year (added as a projection range). Fiscal tables have no separate CBI line. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

2025 Budget Statement (March 2025), 46 pages. Programme content: contingency fund (10 percent of NTF receipts) balance of $44.9 million at 31 December 2024 (added; bare '$', currency recorded as unspecified) and the statement that the set-aside was reduced from 40 to 10 percent (no date; see the April 2023 event from the 2026 Budget Statement); unprecedented CBI inflows behind the 2024 primary surplus (no CBI amount); NTF set-aside for Project Polaris from June 2025 (event added); 70% cut in fees for local developers (event already recorded); regional MoA and regional regulator planned for mid-2026 (events exist); automated certification for CBI citizenship (plan). Reports laid with the budget (contingency fund report, MTEFS) are separate documents, not included in this file. The revenue overview has no separate CBI line. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

Budget book 'Estimates of Revenue and Expenditure 2018' (634 pages; blank divider pages only). Extracted: item 18001 'CBI Fees' (approved 2017 and forward 2019-2020 added; 2017 provisional and 2018 already in the data); 'CBI Committee' dividend line (five columns; the summary on p. 84 prints '-' where p. 80 prints 0 for 2017, noted); NTF grants (Table 5: 46.8m 2017 estimated outturn; Table 10: 81.1m 2018 budget; text says NTF was 48.8% of external financing while the table says 50.5%, shares not recorded); all lines of the NTF capital-source table (PDF p. 92; 48 project lines plus total; lines add up to the totals; the 2017 approved total here is 32,480,000 against 32,380,000 in the 2017 book). Narrative on NTF-financed housing programmes (over EC$5.5m spent and over EC$2m disbursed in 2017; 1,300 and 117 beneficiaries) repeats table lines or counts beneficiaries of spending, not the programme; not recorded separately. Rest of the budget out of scope. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

Budget book 'Estimates of Revenue and Expenditure 2021' (635 pages, text throughout). Extracted: item 18001 'CBI Fees' forward 2022-2023 (other columns already in the data); 'CBI Committee' line; NTF grants (Table 6: 85.7m 2020; Table 10: 172.1m 2021 budget); all lines of the NTF capital-source table (PDF p. 90; 97 projects plus total). Column check: project lines sum to 146,072,030 against a printed approved-2020 total of 146,192,030 (120,000 short) and to 85,675,875 against 85,675,873 (rounding); noted on the total rows. Narrative project paragraphs (pp. 42-45): the M-Power 'EC$4.8 million provided for in 2020' differs from the table's 4,000,000 approved (noted on that row); 'Smart Healthcare Facilities - Grenada Phase 2: Total project cost: EC$1 million funded through NTF' (3-year project, no years, not in the NTF table) is recorded with period basis 'unspecified'. Other project paragraphs do not tie amounts to the NTF. Rest of the budget out of scope. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

Grenada Citizenship by Investment (Amendment) Regulations 2024, S.R.O. 12 of 2024 (4 pages, gazetted 26 June 2024, to commence 1 July 2024): replacement Schedule I with NTF amounts (US$235,000 for main applicant and up to 3 dependants; US$25,000/50,000/75,000 per further dependant by type), approved-project minimum US$350,000, shared unit US$270,000 per share (unit at least US$440,000), government contributions for approved projects and significant investments (US$50,000 plus 25,000/50,000/75,000 per dependant), developer fees (application US$10,000, due diligence US$7,500 for developer and each director, administration US$20,000 a year, start-date extension US$10,000). The four main terms and the price-change event were already recorded; the other 15 amounts are added as program terms. Replaced before commencement by S.R.O. 15 of 2024 (same amounts, unit value corrected to US$540,000). Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

Legislative Council Brief of 19 Dec 2023 on the New CIES: eligibility (age 18+, eligible nationalities, net assets of HK$30m for two years, no adverse record), minimum investment HK$30m (HK$27m permissible assets incl. non-residential real estate capped at HK$10m and certificates of deposit capped at 10%, plus HK$3m in the CIES Investment Portfolio), portfolio maintenance rules, procedure (InvestHK then ImmD; visitor entry up to 180 days to invest; 24-month then 3-year stays; permanent residence after 7 years), buyer's and new residential stamp duty suspension for applicants, implications, planned launch mid-2024. No application statistics. Investment thresholds, Exco approval and the Budget announcement were already recorded; this pass adds the net-asset requirement as a rule row (caps noted in it). Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

InvestHK/FSTB press release of 7 Jan 2025: New CIES enhancements effective 1 Mar 2025 (six-month net-asset test instead of two years, jointly owned assets, holding through a family-owned investment holding vehicle or special purpose entity) and key figures for the first 10 months (enquiries nearly 7,000; applications over 800; 733 passed the net-asset check; 240 passed the investment check; expected investment over HK$24 billion). Also a statement that applications in the first 10 months exceeded those in the same period of the original CIES (no number). The four application figures and the rule-change event were already recorded; this pass adds the enquiries figure (new indicator proposed) and the six-month net-asset rule row. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

Chapter 1 of the ImmD annual report (Visa and Policies): admission schemes and statistics for visitors, employment, talent schemes, students, dependants, one-way permits, right of abode etc. (out of scope) and a section on the Capital Investment Entrant Scheme. CIES section, as at 31 Dec 2011: applications received (entrant and dependant), approvals (formal and in principle), investment $94.9bn (printed twice), the Oct 2010 threshold rise to $10m and suspension of real estate (event already in the dataset from hkg-isd-pr-cies-amended-2010), a planned 2013 review, and the CPA-report count and share. Main figures were already recorded; this pass adds the CPA count and share. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

Chapter 1 of the ImmD annual report (Visa and Policies): admission schemes and statistics for visitors, employment, talent schemes, students, dependants, one-way permits, right of abode etc. (out of scope) and a section on the Capital Investment Entrant Scheme. Chapter 1 of the ImmD annual report (Visa and Policies): admission schemes and statistics for visitors, employment, talent schemes, students, dependants, one-way permits, right of abode etc. (out of scope) and a section on the Capital Investment Entrant Scheme. CIES section, as at 31 Dec 2014: applications received (entrant and dependant), approvals (formal and in principle; parts add up to the printed total), investment total, the Oct 2010 threshold rise and real-estate suspension (event already in the dataset), and the CPA-report count and share. Remark that CIES was suspended from 15 Jan 2015 (event already recorded). Main figures were already recorded; this pass adds the CPA count and share. Chapter 2 (Visa and Policies Branch) of the ImmD Annual Report 2023: visa policy narrative with cumulative or yearly counts for other schemes (GEP, ASMTP, IANG, TechTAS, QMAS, ASSG, labour importation, domestic helpers, students, dependants, one-way permits, certificates of entitlement), all out of scope. CIES paragraph: suspended since 15 Jan 2015; as at 31 Dec 2023, over 35,400 formal approvals and HK$316.9 billion cumulative investment (both already extracted). Dependants of CIES entrants are eligible for dependant visas, but the dependant-visa count is for all schemes (out of scope). New CIES paragraph: implemented 1 March 2024, investment of HK$30 million or more in stocks, funds, bonds etc. 'excluding real estate' (not added: the HK$30m threshold and the launch are already recorded from the LegCo brief and InvestHK; this report's 'excluding real estate' differs from the brief, which lets non-residential real estate count for up to HK$10m). Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

ImmD web announcement (archived Dec 2012) of the CIES rule amendments from 14 Oct 2010: threshold and net-asset requirement raised from HK$6.5m to HK$10m, real estate suspended, Class C insurers allowed as financial intermediaries, three-yearly review, transitional rule for investments made in the six months before; share of entrants who invested before applying (around 11%); cumulative admissions since 2003 (around 8,200 investors, 15,500 dependants, around $58bn); and the separate 6 Jul 2010 refinement admitting investment-linked assurance products (event already recorded). The 14 Oct 2010 threshold change is already an event from hkg-isd-pr-cies-amended-2010. This pass adds the four numbers, the HK$10m rule row and the intermediary event. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

InvestHK press release of 16 Oct 2024: from 16 Oct 2024 residential property counts if a single property costs HK$50 million or more; all real estate together counts for at most HK$10 million; rules updated; details of the 1 March 2025 private-company measure to follow. The HK$50m rule row and the event were already recorded (the HK$10m cap is in that rule row's notes). Nothing added. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

Government press release of 13 Oct 2010: from 14 Oct 2010 threshold raised from HK$6.5m to HK$10m and real estate suspended; insurers allowed as intermediaries; threshold to be reviewed every three years; transitional arrangement; around 11% of entrants invested before applying; since 2003 around 8,200 investors and 15,500 dependants admitted, around $58 billion invested (printed with a bare '$'; the existing row records HKD, following the dataset's practice for Hong Kong Government releases, which is a pending decision). The three cumulative figures, the rule row and the event were already recorded. Added: the 11% share. The insurer change is already an event from hkg-immd-cies-announcement-2012. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

Government press release of 30 Sept 2003: the CIES will accept applications from 27 Oct 2003; HK$6.5 million minimum in real estate and/or specified financial assets; eligible groups (not Mainland residents); six-month investment windows; portfolio maintenance (no top-up if value falls); dependants; right of abode after seven years. No statistics. The rule row and the launch event were already recorded. Nothing added. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

LegCo written reply (23 Feb 2011) on the CIES: question cites applications averaging 570 a month in Jan-Sep 2010 and 242 in Dec 2010, about 1% of property transaction value, and 28 of 2,000 SFC retail funds eligible (press report). Reply: criteria for permissible investment asset classes (five classes of financial assets), reasons for suspending real estate in Oct 2010 and a planned 2013 review, the 70% rule for eligible funds, and a table of average monthly entrants and investment amounts for 2008-2010 with year-on-year changes. All programme numbers extracted; the '28 of 2,000 funds' press figure (a count of eligible products, not a programme outcome) is left as context. The rules described are already covered by existing terms and events. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

Unofficial consolidated Croatian Aliens Act (Zakon o strancima, NN 133/20 to 55/26 per zakon.hr): entry, visas, short stay, temporary residence (family, study, research, etc.), residence and work permits (quotas abolished; employers; seasonal work; art. 110 categories incl. self-employment with 51% ownership and strategic investment projects; art. 113 key staff and self-employed sole owners: EUR 26,544.56 capital or investment, three Croatian employees, salary 1.5 times average; art. 115 strategic investment projects decided within 15 days; validity up to 2 years under art. 110), Blue Card, intra-corporate transfers, long-term residence, return, detention, fines (employer, carrier fines out of scope). Not a passive investor visa. The EUR 26,544.56 threshold was already recorded; employment, salary, ownership and validity conditions added. Employer fines and other permit types are out of scope. No statistics. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

ÁKK programme page (dated 2019-11-18): programme closed 31 March 2017; bond description (from 1 Jan 2015 EUR 50,000 face value, at least 5 years, zero coupon, discount price); only intermediaries contracted with ÁKK could buy; EUR 300,000 per applicant after 1 Jan 2015 held for at least 5 years via the intermediary's security; one intermediary per country approved by Parliament's Economic Committee; contact details; list of the 8 approved intermediaries with committee decision numbers (not counted as a number: the page prints no total), contract terminations of 25 Sep 2014 and 15 Dec 2015 (already events) and the withdrawal of 7 Nov 2016 (added). Added 3 rules and 1 event; EUR 300,000 rule, price change and closure were already in. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

Immigration press release (2 Feb 2026) comparing Global Citizen of Indonesia (GCI, issued January 2026: unlimited stay for ex-citizens, their descendants to the second degree and spouses/children of citizens, report every 5 years, a lighter investment guarantee in bonds, shares, funds, deposits or property, minimum income about USD 1,500 a month or USD 15,000 a year; skills route without investment) with Golden Visa Indonesia (since 2024; 5 or 10 years, renewable; individual investor, corporate investor, second home, global talent, world figures; investment amounts US$2.5m/5m with a company, US$25m/50m corporate, US$350,000/700,000 in bonds, listed shares or deposits). GCI is a diaspora scheme with no programme row and no stated investment amount, so its income figures are not recorded; the six golden visa amounts were already in program_terms; permit validity added. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

Immigration press release (26 Sep 2025): 1,012 golden visas issued to 23 Sep 2025, investment of more than Rp48 trillion (nearly Rp46.5 trillion or about 96% from foreign companies setting up subsidiaries/branches; Rp249.3 billion individual investors; Rp1.45 trillion other golden visa subjects), non-tax revenue Rp12.96 billion, holders from 61 countries, validity 5 to 10 years and benefits. Total, permits, fee revenue and individual-investor amount were already recorded; the other parts, share and nationality count added. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

Opinion of Advocate General Collins of 4 Oct 2024 in C-181/23 Commission v Malta (EUR-Lex XHTML). Legal framework (Maltese Citizenship Act art. 10, 2020 Act and 2020 Regulations: EUR 600,000/750,000 contribution, EUR 10,000 deposit, EUR 700,000 property or EUR 16,000 rent, EUR 10,000 donation, 36 months or 12 months with EUR 150,000 more, EUR 50,000 per dependant, cap of 400 a year and 1,500 in total; 2014 IIP cap of 1,800), pre-litigation steps, parties' arguments, analysis and the proposal to dismiss the action. The scheme terms repeat L.N. 437 of 2020 and are already in program_terms; the opinion event is already recorded under this id. One statement not recorded, for decision: Malta's pleading (point 125 of the text) that "a rate of refusal of approximately one third of all admissible applications" shows the scheme is not automatic; it is a party's claim in words with no period, so it was not turned into a cbi_rejection_rate number. The AG gives the filing date as 22 March 2023 (the judgment says 21 March). Only Malta is covered. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).

Commission report COM(2024) 366 (31 May 2024, 10 pages) on the suspension of the visa exemption for Vanuatu: the schemes since 25 May 2015; Commission concerns 2017-2021; three suspension phases (12 Jan 2022 proposal, 3 Mar 2022 Council decision, 27 Apr 2022 implementing regulation, dialogue meetings, 8 Nov 2022 and 1 Dec 2022 acts, extension to 3 Feb 2025); economic reliance (33% of revenue in 2020 and 2021; 12.3%, 10.2%, 5.3%, 5.5% of GDP 2020-2023; 27% revenue fall in 2022); Table 1 statistics 2015-2021 (14,504 applications, 13,489 citizenships, 10,524 passports, 1,015 rejections/revocations, ~9.6%, 11 main nationalities); inconsistent later data sets (2020: about 4,000 successful to Aug 2020, one refusal, 15 revocations; Jul 2023: 682 and 676 applications; Oct 2023: 144, 127, 130 successful; Mar 2024: 1,072, 875, 1,113 applications with 4, 5, 22 rejections); March 2023 Citizenship Act amendment; restricted nationalities; fees (USD 130,000 single, USD 180,000 couple with two children); no residence requirement; 71 designated agents (60 on the website in April 2024); screening; 2021 name-change ban; February 2023 Commission of enquiry; proposal to move Vanuatu to the visa-required list. Already recorded from this id: "more than 10 000" passports 2015-2021 and the 31 May 2024 event. Added: all Table 1 numbers and nationality rows, the three later data sets, the fiscal shares, agent counts, the 3-month decision deadline and three events (2021 name-change ban, Feb 2023 Commission of enquiry, 21 Mar 2023 amendment). Not added: the fees (same USD 130,000 and 180,000 already recorded from DSP Order No. 33 of 2019 and the Citizenship Office page); the 27% revenue fall (a percentage change, no indicator); the one refusal in 2015-Aug 2020 (words); the earlier suspension dates (already recorded from the EU acts). Table 1 parts do not add to a printed total: the 11 nationalities are "main nationalities" only (8,716 of 13,489). 14,504 applications = 13,489 citizenships + 1,015 rejections/revocations, consistent. Rules restated from other sources are now recorded from this document too (decision 8).
